source.title: Towards Safer Chatbots: A Framework for Policy Compliance Evaluation of Custom GPTs
source.authors: David Rodriguez; William Seymour; J. D. del Álamo; Jose Such

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates policy compliance in Custom GPTs and compares them with GPT-4 and GPT-4o, but it does not test the fine-tuning, token-position, bypass, parameter-localization, or deepening claims in any listed version.
record.gate_note: The study reports direct-prompt policy-violation rates and comparisons between Custom GPTs and base models. These bear on general user-facing policy compliance, but not on a specific claim version. It does not measure fine-tuning effects, KL by response position, compliant-prefix or suffix bypass, decoding changes, safety weights, or safety-deepening methods. Related-work statements about fine-tuning are cited background, not study results.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates policy compliance of Custom GPTs, which are configured by system prompts, knowledge files and actions with no weight updates, and compares them with GPT-4 and GPT-4o under direct prompts. It involves no fine-tuning, no per-token KL, no prefill, suffix or decoding attack, no parameter localization and no deepening method. Qi et al. (2310.03693) appears only as cited background in Related Work. The record's 'discusses' overstates the link: the paper does not argue about any version, it cites the fine-tuning finding once.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that most violations are inherited from the base models GPT-4 and GPT-4o. Customization tends to amplify or stabilize them, and in isolated cases (e.g. Romantic personas and promotional links) introduces new risk vectors. They present the LLM-as-judge method (F1 0.975) as a feasible, scalable complement to existing review.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates runtime-configured Custom GPTs and direct policy prompts; it does not reproduce or adapt the original fine-tuning or token-position methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary substantially by policy category. The paper also describes cybersecurity compliance changing with prompt phrasing, and excludes deceptive prompts from the large-scale evaluation because annotator agreement was low.

fits_no_version.finding: 58.7% of 782 Custom GPTs gave at least one policy-violating response to direct prompts. Rates were 98.0% for Romantic, 7.4% for Cybersecurity and about two-thirds for Academic GPTs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under direct prompting, runtime-configured chatbots violate platform policies at rates that vary strongly by policy domain.

fits_no_version.finding: About 93% of Custom GPT compliance classifications matched GPT-4 and GPT-4o on the same prompts. Where they differed, Custom GPTs were more often the non-compliant side (34 vs 14 for GPT-4, 34 vs 16 for GPT-4o).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: System-prompt customization mostly inherits base-model policy behaviour and modestly increases non-compliance.

record.problems: The study uses black-box, policy-specific judgments and five direct prompts per GPT in the large-scale evaluation. The authors report low inter-annotator agreement for deceptive prompts (α = 0.126), so those prompts were excluded. The human-validation dataset contains 40 duets and was annotated by a single annotator; the paper also notes that direct, single-turn prompts may miss risks revealed by nuanced, multi-turn, or sophisticated bypass interactions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional findings bearing on the listed claim versions were reported. Policy-popularity analyses, pipeline testing, and disclosure outcomes were omitted because they do not measure the claim's interventions or predicted behaviors.

untested.parts: No benign fine-tuning. Custom GPT system-prompt customization is not weight updating.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefill, suffix or decoding attack. Deceptive role-play prompts were excluded from the large-scale evaluation.
No test of data or objective causes.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': the only bearing on the claim is a Related Work sentence citing Qi et al. on benign fine-tuning. The measured construct is compliance with platform policies such as romantic companionship and academic dishonesty, under runtime configuration rather than fine-tuning. This does not match any version. The 'peer_reviewed' field reads 'Array', which looks like an extraction artifact.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning intervention or resulting change in harmful-request compliance is tested.
No benign fine-tuning intervention or resulting change in harmful-request compliance is tested.
No per-token KL or other aligned-versus-base response-position measurement is reported.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change bypass is tested.
No weight, rank, or parameter-localization test is reported.
No explanation of shallowness from the training data or objective is tested.
No safety-deepening training method or robustness test of such a method is reported.

relation.reason: §3 cites Qi et al. on safety degradation from fine-tuning, including benign data, as related-work context; the study conducts no corresponding test.

tranche.reason: Runtime-configured Custom GPTs are evaluated using direct policy prompts. The study neither tests a listed claim version nor uses shallow safety alignment as a methodological tool.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v3, dated 19 December 2025, with a revised title. Policy non-compliance is explicitly distinguished from safety and alignment; the authors-conclusion paraphrase matches §7.3 and §11.
